rows.en: The ways of midrash and halakhah of Hillel and Shammai. Akavya ben Mahalalel.

From the event that befell Hillel with the elders of Betera it follows for us that the study of the Torah was in a very bad state at that time. For we saw that by reason and by the ways of midrash Hillel's proofs were conclusive and compelling from the sense of the words of the written Torah. Nevertheless the Benei Betera refused to listen to his proofs, and their minds were not at rest until he told them that he had received it so from his teachers. Experience teaches us that reliance on what is received without examination and criticism, and clinging to the utterance of the ancients even when compelling proofs point to the opposite, is a sign of slackness in study and of the lack of any scientific effort. But for this reason we shall not say that the cause why the halakhah was hidden from the Benei Betera was none other than that they inclined to the way of the Sadducees, to interpret the verses according to the strict depth of their plain sense (R. Menaḥem ha-Meiri, in the introduction to Avot). Rather, they were Pharisees to the utmost degree, and kept the teaching of the elders with precision and great care; but because they clung with all their strength to the teaching of the elders, it was enough for them to accept a halakhah if its foundation was a tradition from the elders, and they paid no attention to whether one could bring a proof for the tradition from the midrash of Scripture or not. But the widening of the midrash of Scripture, which came forth from the house of study of Shemaiah and Avtalyon and reached perfection under the hands of Hillel, was caused precisely by the complaint of the Sadducees, who said to the Pharisees that their whole teaching, which they had received from the elders, was the work of human hands. Therefore they strove to show them that the teaching of the elders has a foundation and a root in the written Torah, and in this they succeeded with the help of the middot and the ways of their midrash; and perhaps they hoped that the Sadducees too would now consider with understanding and their minds would be at rest. To reach this aim, Hillel's first way was to train the students and the learners to set all their attention on the study of the Torah, to understand and to know how most of the halakhot are founded in the Torah, and to remove the perverse lips of the Sadducees from their teaching. And the later generations rightly compared the work of Hillel in his generation to the work of Ezra in his generation (Sukkah 20a). Yet Hillel's charge was harder than Ezra's charge. For as a rule it is harder to repair the breaches of a great building and to heal its breaks than to found the building and set it up from the foundation to its upper stories.

To reach his aim he used the rules by which the Torah is expounded. Such rules had already served the ancients as aids in their midrashim. These rules were called middot, and they are the foundations of midrash. Hillel gathered them into the number seven and gave them technical names.{v1_09_10:1} These middot are: kal va-ḥomer, gezerah shavah, binyan av, kelal u-ferat, two verses, ka-yotze bo be-makom aḥer, davar ha-lamed me-inyano.{v1_09_10:2} One of the later sages, R. Ishmael, set the middot at thirteen. This number is usual among the masters of the Talmud (Sanhedrin 86a). Of the source from which the middot came, nothing is told us in the Talmud, nor in the other ancient books of the Oral Torah. But in the responsa of the Geonim they ascribed the middot to a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai (*Sefer ha-Keritut*, Batei Middot, Bayit 1:9), and after the Geonim many of the commentators followed this view{v1_09_11:1} without considering how it is possible that the masters of the Talmud, and before them the masters of the Mishnah, held this view and did not hint at it even with a slight hint in any place. If they found a place to publish that black straps are a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai, how did they not find a place in the great and wide sea of the Talmud to publish likewise this great principle on which the whole teaching of the sages in the Talmud rests? It is true that one cannot deny their antiquity with regard to their essence, since most of them rest on reasoning, and reasoning is the offspring of the intellect; therefore, from the time the Torah was written, the intellect was surely the instrument that would help us reach its nature. But with regard to their being technical rules, gathered into a particular number and under particular names, the matter is clear: Hillel or his teachers investigated and inquired into the midrashim of the Torah that had been expounded up to their time, considered the manners of the expositions and their nature, and found that these expositions were founded on such-and-such a course of reasoning; and to make it easier for the expounders they collected and arranged these foundations and gave them fitting names, and their number came out to seven. In the course of time, in proportion as exposition and inquiry increased, various rules also increased, and each rule by itself widened until it passed its first boundary; and because of this we find that as exposition went further in time, the nature of the midrashim changed more and more. This passing of the boundary is found in the middah of gezerah shavah in a remarkable manner. This middah in its essence is a principle laid down in the logic of language, for the likeness of the words is the faithful witness to the likeness of the matters, and this is the nature of gezerah shavah in essence. But this middah needs much caution, for there is no middah by which we can become entangled in errors as much as by gezerah shavah, because similar words are many in the Torah (Yerushalmi Pesaḥim 6:1). For this reason the ancients decreed that a man may not expound a gezerah shavah on his own, but it must be received [by tradition] from the great court of the generation (*Kin'at ha-Emet* by R. Ḥ. Ḥagiz, root 2), because what is agreed in the great court comes from the opinions of the great men of the generation, and on them we can rely that they surely did not pass their bounds. But the sages of the later generations loosened the strap and expounded by gezerah shavah in a way that goes beyond the bounds of the rule of logic, and from this were born strange midrashim that the plain sense of Scripture cannot bear. And what happened to gezerah shavah happened also to all the other middot, and especially to the exposition of ribbui and mi'ut [inclusion and exclusion].{v1_09_11:2} Besides the middot that were counted, they had further sound rules that served them as aids in the interpretation of the Torah. These rules are scattered in the books of the Oral Torah, and some of them are hinted at in the midrashim of the ancients.{v1_09_11:3} One is the middah of hekkesh [analogy]. By it Hillel expounded before the elders of Betera (Pesaḥim 66a, and the Yerushalmi), and Hillel did not count it among his middot because it is included in the middah of davar ha-lamed me-inyano (*Sefer Keritut*, Batei Middot, Bayit 2). And this hekkesh that Hillel expounded is a rational exposition. For he proves that the Passover offering overrides the Sabbath by comparing the Passover offering to the daily offering: just as the Sabbath does not stand in the way of the daily offering, since it is a public offering, so the Passover offering, which is a public offering, should by right override the Sabbath. There are many such analogies in the midrashim that are rational and agree with the plain sense of Scripture.{v1_09_12:1} But in the course of time matters were compared to one another that have no likeness in their nature and are sometimes opposites, and there is no inner reason to equate them, only that they are written next to each other in the Torah.{v1_09_12:2} From the middah of hekkesh came forth the middah of semukhim [juxtaposition], of which the ancients knew nothing.{v1_09_12:3} Such was also the lot of other middot: not only were they moved from their first, rational nature, but they were fruitful and multiplied and gave birth to new middot that the ancients had not imagined. The middah that was moved furthest from its nature is the middah of ribbui and mi'ut. This middah is in essence rational. For it is clear that if there is found in the Torah a superfluity of some statement or of a word that is understood by itself, this superfluity was not written by chance and without a particular intention, especially in statements of statutes and judgments; and if such a superfluity is found, every interpreter will try to understand the particular intention that the lawgiver intended by that superfluity. To make the matter clear to us, let us consider as an example one statute in the Torah, the statute of the forgotten oath, of which it is said: “Or if a soul swear, pronouncing with his lips to do evil or to do good, whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with an oath, and it be hid from him ... and he shall bring his guilt offering unto the Lord” (Leviticus 5:4). Now the words “to do evil or to do good” cannot be understood in any other way than either that he swore to do evil or to do good to others, or that he swore to do evil or to do good to himself (Talmud and Sifra). But as for what Scripture added, saying “whatsoever it be that a man shall pronounce with his lips,”⚠1 it is clear that by this addition it meant to include also things in which there is neither harm nor benefit, and that it spoke of harm and benefit only as the usual case. This interpretation is the plain sense of Scripture and is founded on the middah of ribbui. Likewise the middah of mi'ut is a natural feature of the style of speech in general, and of the style of statutes and judgments in particular, for the lawgiver speaks with precision, and if he specifies particular details he wants to exclude other details that were not specified. And are there not words in the language whose essential meaning is nothing other than the exclusion of something from things, such as the words rak, akh and the like? Therefore it is clear that ribbui and mi'ut in their root are natural features of language. But in the course of time inclusions and exclusions were made “that we know not”⚠2 [cf. Deuteronomy 32:17],{v1_09_12:4} and new derivatives came forth from them, which were also counted as middot and were an aid to the midrash of the Torah. These derivatives are: “There is no inclusion after inclusion except to exclude; there is no exclusion after exclusion except to include” (Sifra Vayikra, parashah 10; Menaḥot 74a). But the derivatives are no longer rational like their fathers in their root. In short, if we pay attention to the rules and the ways of exposition that the later sages had, we find that they flowed from the middot of the earlier ones and are nothing but widenings; only the widenings went so far from the nature of the root that their root is no longer recognizable.

rows.en: The sages who came after the Talmud considered the expositions of the masters of the Talmud and found how strange their interpretations were and how far they were from the plain sense of Scripture, and they found no defense except by saying that they did not intend to interpret Scripture, but that all the strange midrashim that depart from the plain sense are asmakhtot [mere supports].{v1_09_13:1} But whoever considers the language of the ancient sages will find that it is not so. For in all the halakhic midrashim we find that they used the expressions “What does Scripture teach us,” “Scripture comes to teach you,” “Therefore it is said,” “From where do you say,” “Why is it said,” and many expressions like these; and how can it enter the mind that they intended only to give a support for a matter? Likewise we see that in most of their expositions the sages disagreed, each one expounding the verse in a different way, or even opposing one another from one extreme to the other; and how is it possible that the main point of the midrash was said only as an asmakhta? What use is there in whether one supports the matter on the verse in this way or in another? Likewise we find in many places one technical phrase that is usual among the sages of the Mishnah: when they bring a halakhah together with the midrash that points to it, their way is to say, “From here they said such-and-such.” The intention of this is plain: from the midrash of that verse flows the halakhah such-and-such. So the midrash is the source of the halakhah, and if the verse had not been expounded in this way the halakhah would not have been said. Thus we see that the midrash is not an asmakhta but the interpretation of Scripture. Indeed, where the sages themselves thought that the midrash was only an asmakhta, they did not refrain from saying so explicitly, and they said: “From here the sages found support for this matter from the Torah,” or they would say: “A hint for such-and-such a matter from the Torah.” Therefore it is clear that the midrash of Scripture was for them the interpretation of Scripture, and every expounder thought that this was truly the intention of the text. And let it not be a wonder in our eyes that most of the midrashim seem to us like strange interpretations. For it is not right for us to judge their ways of midrash and the plain sense of Scripture in their times by the measure we have for the nature of the plain sense of Scripture. For the recognition of the plain sense changes according to the state of knowledge of the language in which the interpreted book was written, according to the recognition of the matters and rules needed to understand the book, and above all according to the level of enlightenment in the time and place of its writing. Because of this, the plain interpretation changes in proportion to the change of that state. If we consider the ways of interpretation of the commentators up to this day, we find a great difference in the understanding of the plain sense of Scripture, and as a rule what was called the plain sense in one generation was strange in the eyes of the generation that came after it. Even among the sages of one generation the opinions were not always the same in recognizing the plain sense, for the nature of the interpreter's soul also gives its nature to the thing interpreted. So it was among the Tannaim: R. Ishmael did not accept the plain sense of R. Akiva, nor the reverse, and so among the other Tannaim. From this were born disputes in the interpretation of the verses, until they sometimes said to one another, “How long will you heap up [words] or twist the text?” And one of the later sages (Rava) said: Although in the whole Torah a verse does not depart from its plain sense, nevertheless we find that a gezerah shavah comes and takes the verse out of its plain sense entirely (Yevamot 24a). According to this view, the whole Torah that is expounded does not depart from its plain sense by means of midrash, and if one of the middot takes the verse out of its plain sense, then the matter is noted specially because of the novelty in it. Already at the end of the days of the sages of the Talmud they had a slight feeling that the midrashim of the sages, as they had developed in time, were no longer truly the plain sense of Scripture. Of Rav Kahana (the second) it is told that he said of himself that already when he was eighteen years old he was versed in the whole Talmud, but he did not know that a verse does not depart from its plain sense, until his companion Mar son of Ravina informed him that all the midrashim of the sages are the plain sense of Scripture (Shabbat 63a). There are indeed midrashim that are not complete, and of these the sages said: “It is a mere asmakhta.” Likewise they sometimes gave a hint for a matter of halakhah in Scripture (Kiddushin 80b, and in many places). Likewise they sometimes expounded a verse in the manner of rhetoric and hung a moral matter on it (Ketubbot 111b), or they used the language of Scripture in conversation between a man and his fellow, but with an intention other than its plain sense (Ḥullin 6a; see also there 133a), or by way of a parable on a matter of halakhah (Arakhin 8b). In all these they said explicitly that the plain sense of the verse is to be understood with another intention. Yet in all these places the plain sense of the verse is also brought beside the homiletic interpretation; and if we consider this interpretation to which they give the name “the plain sense of the verse,” we find that it does not differ from the whole mass of midrashim that exist, and it did not occur to the plain-sense interpreters after the Talmud that one of them would follow, in interpreting the plain sense, the interpretations that were called by them the plain sense of Scripture. This is what I said: that the midrash of the verses according to their ways and their middot was for them the plain sense of Scripture.

footnotes.en: There a story is told of a man whose sons did not behave properly toward him, and he wrote his property over to Jonathan ben Uzziel. What did Jonathan ben Uzziel do? He sold a third, consecrated a third, and returned a third to the man's sons. Shammai came upon him with his staff and his bag. He said to him: Shammai, you cannot take back what I have sold, etc. And Shammai said: Ben Uzziel has rebuffed me. Rashbam explains “with his staff and his bag” as: to dispute with him. From this the scholar Graetz concluded that Shammai went out against him with a staff to compel him, and that this is a sign of his irascibility. But the intention of the baraita is not so. In my opinion one should judge the reverse: from the fact that Shammai went to him and did not summon him to come before him, as is the way of a master with a disciple, it is shown that he dealt with him in humility. And as for his coming with his staff and his bag, one should not explain that he came with a staff to chastise him and compel him, for if so, why his bag? Rather, the phrase “came with his staff and his bag” is a standing expression everywhere for describing setting out on a journey, as in Shabbat (31a): “This proselyte came with his staff and his bag”; and in Rosh Hashanah chapter 2, in the story of Rabban Gamaliel, we find “he took his staff and his money in his hand.” And as for the author of the statement using the word “upon him,” which implies that he came upon him with a staff to chastise him, as in “that you come to me with staves” [1 Samuel 17:43], said in the story of Goliath, such a fine point is not enough to take the phrase “came with his staff and his bag” out of its plain sense. But know that the whole story is told in the Yerushalmi, Nedarim end of chapter 4, in another manner and the very reverse of what is told in the Bavli; therefore it is hard to draw conclusions from it for the benefit of history.

In Graetz's opinion Shemaiah and Avtalyon were natives of Alexandria; and according to this conjecture the opinion of R. Aaron Jellinek is right, that these sages may have been versed in Greek wisdom and known the rules of Aristotle's logic, and that on that model they too brought order into the middot of the Torah, gave them names and gathered them into a number, and from them Hillel received the order of the middot, their number and their names. But if so, it would have been fitting to ascribe the middot to Shemaiah and Avtalyon.

In the Sifra, at the end of the Baraita of R. Ishmael, the middot of Hillel are counted, and these are: kal va-ḥomer, gezerah shavah, two verses, kelal u-ferat, ka-yotze bo be-makom aḥer, davar ha-lamed me-inyano. One is missing from the count. In Avot de-Rabbi Natan chapter 37 it counts: kal va-ḥomer, gezerah shavah, binyan av from one verse, binyan av from two verses, kelal u-ferat, perat u-khelal, ka-yotze bo be-makom aḥer, davar ha-lamed me-inyano; and in this count there is one extra. In Tosefta Sanhedrin chapter 7 the reading is as in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, except that in place of kelal u-ferat, perat u-khelal it counts kelal u-ferat u-khelal⚠1; so there is no addition. It seems to me that the main reading is that of the Sifra, except that binyan av has dropped out. See what I wrote above in chapters 16, 17, 19, together with what we saw of the particular middot by which Hillel expounded, and you will find that the middot counted in the Sifra, as I have corrected it, are found in the midrashim of the ancients.

1.note: Read as kelal u-ferat u-khelal (one middah); could also be meant as two items, ‘kelal u-ferat’ and ‘kelal’.

footnotes.en: Rashi on Sukkah (31a), Gittin (41b), Niddah (19a) followed the Geonim, and so did Maimonides in his introduction to the Mishnah. And the Rabad⚠1 in his commentary on the Baraita of R. Ishmael wrote that the tradition is the father of them all, except two that are explicit in the Torah, namely kal va-ḥomer and the two contradicting verses; and he was careful not to say that they are a halakhah [given] to Moses at Sinai, because there is no proof from the Talmud; and see Tosafot Zevaḥim (28b). This is also the opinion of Naḥmanides in his glosses to the *Sefer ha-Mitzvot*, root 2; and how much the master strained to picture in what manner the halakhah was handed down! Others have already tried to describe this matter and did not succeed. See Rashi Kiddushin (17a), s.v. Mikhah, and Tosafot Shabbat (97a), s.v. Gezerah shavah; and see the commentary ascribed to Rashi on Ta'anit (20a).

The middah of ribbui was expounded by the early elders (Mekhilta, tractate de-Amalek, chapter 5). “And the scall be healed” [Leviticus 13:37]: and not that a scall within a scall [is excluded] (that is, that this is unclean); or the reading⚠1 “to include a scall within a scall” (meaning: for uncleanness). So Hillel expounded (Sifra Tazria, chapter 9; see there in my work *Masoret ha-Talmud*.

footnotes.en: Of this kind is the analogy: “This is the law of the meal offering” [Leviticus 6:7] — one law for all the meal offerings (Sifra Tzav, chapter 2); and the analogy of two matters by means of the kaf of comparison, as “as the sin offering, as the guilt offering” [Leviticus 6:10] (ibid., chapter 9, and Zevaḥim 11b, see there); see also Zevaḥim (98a), Menaḥot (83a), and in *Masoret ha-Talmud*, parashat Aḥarei, chapter 3, letter resh.

Such as the analogy of becoming [married] to going out [divorce], Sifre Ki Tetze, section 268; Kiddushin, Yerushalmi 1:1, and the Bavli there. The analogy of the kinds of becoming [betrothal] to one another (Ketubbot 46b). He compares disputes to plagues (Niddah 50a). From the force of the middah of hekkesh also came the midrash: “then they shall both of them die” [Deuteronomy 22:22] — that both of them be equal (Sanhedrin 66b).

Of the middah of semukhim we have not found among the ancients even a slight hint. There is no doubt that it is a derivative of hekkesh: from the time that the very idea in the middah of hekkesh was no longer grasped, and they compared matters to one another because Scripture included them and wrote them together, from then on they thought that the juxtaposition of matters is also fit to be expounded. In no exposition did they pass the bound of the plain sense as in the middah of semukhim, and rightly R. Judah said (Yevamot 4a): “Because they juxtaposed this matter, shall we take this woman out to burning?” In several places we find that the masters of the Talmud, through their holding to the middah of semukhim, sometimes understood some midrash in a baraita as though it was expounded by juxtaposition, and added to the baraita the words “and juxtaposed to it,” as: “and juxtaposed to it: if for a thanksgiving” [Leviticus 7:12] (Kiddushin 53a), and in the Sifra Tzav chapter 10 it is not there. Likewise we find in Pesaḥim (28b): “and juxtaposed to it: this day you go out” [Exodus 13:4], and in the Mekhilta Bo chapter 16 it is not there; and see there what I wrote in *Middot Soferim*, letter lamed; and so it is in many places.

From the middot of ribbui and mi'ut came forth derivatives in which most of the midrashim of the later sages are included. They extended them even to letters, and even to the dots in the Torah. And of R. Akiva⚠1 they said that he would expound heaps upon heaps of halakhot on every single tittle. The words “kol, gam, af, akh, rak, et, o, hu, hi” they expounded, each according to its true meaning, to include or to exclude. But they greatly overstepped the measure, and many strange midrashim came forth. For example, let us take the exposition of “kol” to include: if R. Eliezer said that “any [kol] leaven ... [you shall not] burn” [Leviticus 2:11] is to include part of it (Menaḥot 58a), or if we include blemished priests in the distribution of holy things from “every [kol] male among the sons of Aaron shall eat it” [Leviticus 6:11] (Zevaḥim 102a), the plain sense of the verse does not contradict this. But if R. Akiva expounds that all disqualified holy things are [to be] burned, from the words “and every [kol] sin offering” [Leviticus 6:23] (ibid. 82a), this does not bear the plain sense of Scripture; on the contrary, its reverse is its plain sense, as R. Yose the Galilean answered him. Likewise, if we expound (Sifra Tzav chapter 10 and Pesaḥim 43b) from “for whoever [kol] eats the fat” [Leviticus 7:25] to include the fat of blemished animals, this is not its plain sense but an inversion of the verse, as though it were written “whoever eats any fat.” Likewise they expounded ribbui and mi'ut from single letters, such as he, vav, mem; see Yevamot (54a), Kiddushin (9b, 41a); and in Sanhedrin (51b) R. Akiva expounded a vav and R. Ishmael answered him; see also there (14a), Tosafot s.v. ve-R. Shimon; and see Sotah (28a). All these do not fit with the plain sense of Scripture. The exposition of mi'ut by the letter mem has its root in the plain sense of Scripture, for we have found many mems whose meaning is partitive; but we cannot give this meaning to every serving mem that stands for min. Therefore, if one excludes by the mem of “of the blood of the bull” [Leviticus 4:5] — and not the blood of the flesh, etc. (Sifra Vayikra, Dibbura de-Nedavah chapter 3; Zevaḥim 25a), one cannot contradict this from the side of the plain sense of Scripture. But if we expound “if any of their carcass fall” [Leviticus 11:37]: some of their carcass makes unclean and some does not make unclean, excluding a dry one that cannot be soaked (Sifra Shemini, chapter 11); or “if any of the beasts die” [Leviticus 11:39]: some of the beasts make unclean and some of the beasts do not make unclean, excluding a terefah that was slaughtered (ibid., parashah 10), on this the plain-sense interpreter will say: if it is an exposition, expound it; but this is not the plain sense of Scripture. And the disciples of R. Akiva expounded the dots, and no doubt they received this from R. Akiva their master; see Pesaḥim (94b), Menaḥot 87b, and see also Nazir (23a).

footnotes.en: This is the opinion of Ibn Ezra in many places; and see Maimonides in his Roots, root 2, and Naḥmanides in his glosses disagrees with him; and see Tosafot Eruvin 23b, s.v. Peshitei, from whose words it follows that every exposition that is not according to the plain sense of the verse is an asmakhta; and hence it is proved that every complete exposition is the plain sense of the verse. And see *Mikhtav Itti* of R. A. G.⚠1, part 5, p. 67.
